intro: Japanese keeps the verb, and its negative, for the very end of the sentence. These adverbs are an early signal: once a speaker says 全然, めったに or 必ずしも, the listener already knows a 'not' is coming, and the sentence must deliver it. Each adverb also says what kind of 'not' it is: how much (全然, あまり), how often (めったに), how well (ろくに), how universally (必ずしも, 一切), how stubbornly (なかなか) or how unthinkably (まさか). Choose by asking which of these the sentence is about, then make sure the ending matches.

skills.rule: Not at all is 全然〜ない (everyday) or ちっとも〜ない (spoken, with feeling); not very or not much is あまり〜ない; never, by no means, as a vow or firm judgement, is 決して〜ない.
skills.explain:
全然 ('not at all') is the everyday zero: 全然わからない, 全然寒くない. ちっとも means the same but is spoken and emotional, often a complaint about something that should be happening: 弟はちっとも手伝わない. Keep it out of formal writing.

あまり (casual あんまり) is a softer 'not very, not much, not often': あまり寒くない is a little cold, 全然寒くない is not cold at all. Without a negative, あまりに(も) means 'too': あまりにも高い.

決して is not about quantity. It is a firm promise, warning or judgement: 決して忘れません, 決して諦めないでください, 決して簡単ではない. To report that something simply did not happen, use 全然.

In casual speech 全然 is also heard with positives (全然大丈夫, 'totally fine'); in standard and written Japanese, and in this drill, it takes the negative.
patterns: 全然 / ちっとも [verb / adjective in the negative]
あまり [verb / adjective in the negative] (not very, not much)
決して [negative of a promise, warning or judgement]

examples.jp: 今日[きょう]は{あまり}寒[さむ]くないです。
examples.en: It isn't very cold today.

examples.jp: 漢字[かんじ]が{全然[ぜんぜん]}読[よ]めません。
examples.en: I can't read kanji at all.

examples.jp: 最近[さいきん]は{あまり}映画[えいが]を見[み]ていません。
examples.en: I haven't been watching many films lately.

examples.jp: 弟[おとうと]は{ちっとも}部屋[へや]を片付[かたづ]けない。
examples.en: My brother never tidies his room, not one bit.

examples.jp: このご恩[おん]は{決[けっ]して}忘[わす]れません。
examples.en: I will never forget your kindness.

examples.jp: 外国語[がいこくご]を覚[おぼ]えるのは{決[けっ]して}簡単[かんたん]ではない。
examples.en: Learning a foreign language is by no means easy.

contrast.note: とても intensifies a positive: とても寒い. 'Not very cold' is あまり寒くない. With a negative potential, とても means 'can't possibly' (とても食べられない), not 'not very'.
よく means 'often' or 'well' and goes with a positive. Its negative partner is あまり: よく行く / あまり行かない.
全然 measures how much: 全然食べていない (I've eaten nothing). 決して declares a stance: 決して食べない (I will never eat it).

mistakes.bad: 日本語[にほんご]は{とても}話[はな]せません。
mistakes.good: 日本語[にほんご]は{あまり}話[はな]せません。
mistakes.note: To say 'I can't speak it very well', use あまり + negative; とても + a negative potential means 'I can't possibly speak it'.

mistakes.bad: この映画[えいが]は{全然[ぜんぜん]}面白[おもしろ]い。
mistakes.good: この映画[えいが]は{全然[ぜんぜん]}面白[おもしろ]くない。
mistakes.note: In standard Japanese 全然 announces a negative, so the ending must be negative.

mistakes.bad: 昨日[きのう]は{決[けっ]して}寝[ね]られなかった。
mistakes.good: 昨日[きのう]は{全然[ぜんぜん]}寝[ね]られなかった。
mistakes.note: Reporting how little something happened is 全然; 決して is for vows and firm judgements.

skills.tip: Zero → 全然 (ちっとも if you are complaining). A little → あまり. Never, as a promise or verdict → 決して. Then check the verb ends in ない.

skills.rule: Hardly ever is めったに〜ない; not properly is ろくに〜ない; not necessarily is 必ずしも〜とは限らない / わけではない; none whatsoever is 一切〜ない.
skills.explain:
めったに is about frequency: something happens so rarely it is almost never. 父はめったに怒らない. Its opposite is よく.

ろくに is about quality: something was not done properly or enough, and the speaker is unhappy about it. ろくに寝ていない, ろくに読まずにサインした.

必ずしも makes a partial negative: 'not always, not necessarily'. It does not deny the statement, only that it holds every time, so the ending is とは限らない, わけではない or ではない: 高い物が必ずしもいいとは限らない. Do not confuse it with 必ず ('without fail'), which goes with positives.

一切 is total and categorical: not a single one of a category, typically in rules, official statements and firm refusals: 一切関係ありません, 返品は一切受け付けません. It negates things and actions, not degrees: for 'not cold at all' say 全然寒くない. As a noun, 一切 means 'everything' (一切を任せる), a separate use.
patterns: めったに [verb in the negative] (rarely)
ろくに [verb in the negative] (not properly)
必ずしも [statement] とは限らない / わけではない
一切 [verb in the negative] (none whatsoever)

examples.jp: 父[ちち]は{めったに}怒[おこ]りません。
examples.en: My father hardly ever gets angry.

examples.jp: この辺[へん]では雪[ゆき]は{めったに}降[ふ]らない。
examples.en: It rarely snows around here.

examples.jp: 忙[いそが]しくて、昨日[きのう]は{ろくに}食事[しょくじ]もできなかった。
examples.en: I was so busy yesterday that I couldn't even eat properly.

examples.jp: 高[たか]い物[もの]が{必[かなら]ずしも}いいとは限[かぎ]らない。
examples.en: Expensive things are not necessarily good.

examples.jp: 当店[とうてん]はこの件[けん]とは{一切[いっさい]}関係[かんけい]ありません。
examples.en: This shop has nothing whatsoever to do with this matter.

contrast.note: よく (often) and いつも (always) take positives. 'Rarely' is めったに〜ない; 'not always' is いつも〜とは限らない or 必ずしも〜とは限らない.
きっと and 必ず assert that something will happen. 必ずしも does the opposite: it denies that it always happens.
全然 is everyday and grades anything, adjectives included. 一切 is formal and categorical, for whole classes of things or actions: 連絡は一切ない.

mistakes.bad: 田中[たなか]さんは{めったに}遅刻[ちこく]します。
mistakes.good: 田中[たなか]さんは{めったに}遅刻[ちこく]しません。
mistakes.note: めったに only works with a negative ending: 'hardly ever is late'.

mistakes.bad: この薬[くすり]は{必[かなら]ずしも}効[き]きます。
mistakes.good: この薬[くすり]は{必[かなら]ずしも}効[き]くとは限[かぎ]りません。
mistakes.note: 必ずしも needs a partial negative ending such as とは限らない or わけではない.

mistakes.bad: 今日[きょう]は{一切[いっさい]}寒[さむ]くない。
mistakes.good: 今日[きょう]は{全然[ぜんぜん]}寒[さむ]くない。
mistakes.note: 一切 rules out every item of a category; it does not grade an adjective.

skills.tip: How often → めったに. How well → ろくに. Not every time → 必ずしも ... とは限らない. Not a single one, officially → 一切.

skills.rule: With a negative, なかなか means something wanted or expected just won't happen or takes ages; with a positive evaluation, it means 'quite, better than expected'.
skills.explain:
Negative use: なかなか〜ない describes resistance. You are waiting or trying, and the thing keeps not happening: バスがなかなか来ない, 子供がなかなか寝ない, この漢字はなかなか覚えられない. It implies that it should happen and eventually may. 全然来ない says there is no sign of it at all; なかなか来ない says it is taking far too long.

Positive use: なかなか + an evaluative adjective or noun means 'quite, pretty, surprisingly': なかなかおいしい, なかなか上手だ, なかなかの腕前. It suggests 'better than I expected', so it is mild praise, and it sounds condescending if you use it to judge a superior's work.

There is no third use: with an ordinary positive verb it is wrong (×なかなか来た). With a verb, the ending must be negative.
patterns: なかなか [verb in the negative] (just won't, takes ages)
なかなか [potential verb in the negative] (can't manage to)
なかなか [evaluative adjective] / なかなかの [noun] (quite good)

examples.jp: バスが{なかなか}来[こ]ない。
examples.en: The bus just isn't coming.

examples.jp: この漢字[かんじ]は{なかなか}覚[おぼ]えられません。
examples.en: I just can't seem to memorise this kanji.

examples.jp: 子供[こども]が{なかなか}寝[ね]てくれなくて、困[こま]っています。
examples.en: My child takes ages to fall asleep, and it's wearing me out.

examples.jp: この店[みせ]のラーメンは{なかなか}おいしいね。
examples.en: The ramen here is pretty good, isn't it?

examples.jp: 初[はじ]めてにしては、{なかなか}上手[じょうず]だよ。
examples.en: That's quite good for a first try.

contrast.note: すぐ says it happens right away: バスがすぐ来た. なかなか〜ない is its opposite: it keeps not happening.
全然来ない: there is no sign of it at all. なかなか来ない: it is expected but taking too long.
とても is a plain 'very'. なかなか with a positive is 'quite, better than expected', an evaluation, not a neutral intensifier.

mistakes.bad: 電車[でんしゃ]が{なかなか}来[き]た。
mistakes.good: 電車[でんしゃ]が{なかなか}来[こ]なかった。
mistakes.note: With a verb, なかなか only works in the negative: 'the train took ages to come'.

mistakes.bad: 部長[ぶちょう]、今日[きょう]の発表[はっぴょう]は{なかなか}よかったです。
mistakes.good: 部長[ぶちょう]、今日[きょう]の発表[はっぴょう]はとても勉強[べんきょう]になりました。
mistakes.note: Positive なかなか grades someone's work as 'not bad'; aimed at a superior it sounds condescending.

skills.tip: Verb in the slot after it? Then it must end in ない and mean 'just won't'. Adjective of praise? Then it means 'quite good'.

skills.rule: まさか expresses disbelief: 'surely not' with 〜ないだろう / 〜ないよね, and 'I never imagined' with 〜とは思わなかった / 〜とは about something that actually happened.
skills.explain:
まさか marks a possibility as one the speaker can hardly believe. It has three common shapes.

Looking ahead, it rejects a possibility: まさか雨は降らないだろう ('surely it won't rain'). Asking, it checks a fear: まさか会社を辞めるつもりじゃないよね? ('you're not seriously ...?').

Looking back, it reacts to something unbelievable that did happen: まさか彼が落ちるとは思わなかった ('I never dreamt he would fail'). The ending is often cut short to 〜とは: まさかここで会うとは.

Alone, まさか! is 'No way!'. まさかの + noun means 'unexpected': まさかの逆転.

The edge: まさか always carries 'that can't be'. A confident prediction is きっと, a neutral guess is たぶん, a wish or request is ぜひ, and a firm personal vow is 決して.
patterns: まさか [event] ないだろう / ないでしょう (surely not)
まさか [event] んじゃないよね? (you don't mean ...?)
まさか [event] とは思わなかった / とは (never imagined)

examples.jp: 「宝[たから]くじが当[あ]たったよ。」「{まさか}！」
examples.en: "I won the lottery!" "No way!"

examples.jp: こんなに晴[は]れているから、{まさか}雨[あめ]は降[ふ]らないだろう。
examples.en: It's so sunny that surely it won't rain.

examples.jp: {まさか}本当[ほんとう]に会社[かいしゃ]を辞[や]めるつもりじゃないよね。
examples.en: You're not seriously planning to quit the company, are you?

examples.jp: {まさか}彼[かれ]が試験[しけん]に落[お]ちるとは思[おも]わなかった。
examples.en: I never imagined he would fail the exam.

examples.jp: {まさか}こんな所[ところ]で先生[せんせい]に会[あ]うとは。
examples.en: Who would have thought I'd run into my teacher in a place like this!

contrast.note: きっと predicts confidently that it will happen: きっと来る. まさか says it surely won't: まさか来ないだろう.
たぶん is a neutral 'probably' with no surprise. まさか adds 'that would be unthinkable'.
ぜひ is 'by all means' with a wish or request: ぜひ来てください. It never expresses doubt.

mistakes.bad: 彼[かれ]は{まさか}来[く]るでしょう。
mistakes.good: 彼[かれ]は{きっと}来[く]るでしょう。
mistakes.note: A confident positive prediction is きっと; まさか expects the thing not to be true.

mistakes.bad: {まさか}彼[かれ]が優勝[ゆうしょう]した。
mistakes.good: {まさか}彼[かれ]が優勝[ゆうしょう]するとは思[おも]わなかった。
mistakes.note: まさか needs an ending of disbelief: ないだろう, とは思わなかった, or とは.

skills.tip: Is the speaker saying 'that can't be' or 'I never dreamt it'? Then まさか, and the sentence ends in ないだろう or とは (思わなかった).
